title: General and Pathological Personality Traits Overlap Substantially in Children and Teens
abstract:
While personality disorders are diagnosed as categorical syndromes, researchers have 
begun to conceptualize personality disorders as extreme variations of general personality traits. Much evidence supports this hypothesis in adults, but no research has yet tested the relationship between “normal” and “abnormal” traits in children. This study explored this relationship using data collected from 1,370 parent reports of personality in children aged 6 to 17 (Mage=10.1 SD=± 3.36) via short­form questionnaires derived from the Inventory of Individual Child Differences (ICID­-S) and the Dimensional Personality Symptom Item Pool (DIPSI­-SF). Four higher order domains of neuroticism, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and extraversion were scored from the ICID­-S item responses and were hypothesized to correlate significantly with the corresponding DIPSI­-SF dimensions of emotional instability, disagreeableness, compulsivity, and introversion respectively based on prior evidence in adults. Results indicated significant, positive correlations between the ICID­S domain of Neuroticism and the DIPSI­-SF domain of Emotional Instability (r =0.689, p<0.001) and the ICID­S domain of Conscientiousness and the DIPSI­-SF Compulsivity domain (r =0.270, p<0.001). A significant, negative correlation was found between the ICID-­S domain of Agreeableness and the DIPSI-­SF domain of Disagreeableness (r =­0.706, p<0.001), and, surprisingly, no significant correlation was found between the domains of Introversion and Extraversion. Additionally, exploratory analysis of a shared psychoticism dimension did not reveal significant overlap between Openness to Experience and Paranoid Traits. These findings suggest a convergence of measures of personality pathology and normative traits in youth on some common, well ­established domains and call for further exploration of this shared dimensional model.
